Four dense-enabled streams returned at the 25 s client timeout to within 36 ms of each other on all three probes; `debates`, the one stream with no dense leg, returned in 4.0–6.1 s. **Dense retrieval was worth ~12 points of in-stream recall against S13 on the same index (42% → 30%) — a bigger number than anything the merge does.** ▶ Durable finding, written down: **plain rank fusion across streams IS round-robin** (the streams are disjoint — 0 of 10 pairs shared a document on any probe). ⚠ Four defects of my own, all found by measurement: a cost ceiling that refused its own configuration; a reranker output budget that truncated 29 of 64 queries (each naming itself, because §18's guard is in the shared helper); **a model comparison that was never taken because both arms ran `gemini-2.5-pro`** — the harness now compares the ECHOED model on every call, and **the corrected comparison reversed my own choice: Flash is 11.5× cheaper, 22× faster and better on both recall figures, so the registry default moved to it**; and a rank-decay of 0.35 that made one source take 19.9 of 20 slots on 40 of 40 questions, corrected to 0.07 from the arithmetic. ✅ `check:s14-merge` 20 assertions, 10 negative controls, all watched firing. handoff. The core of it is three vote-ish mechanisms that must not collapse into one: a QUESTION vote
is up-only and self-voting is ALLOWED because it records frequency ("I get asked this too"), not
quality; an ANSWER vote is up/down, mutually exclusive and self-voting is refused; a FAVOURITE is
private and is never counted, ranked, aggregated or shown to anyone, admins included — the check
asserts that absence rather than trusting it. ⚠ One deliberate correction to the design pack, per the
brief: favourites in packs are ADDITIVE, not substitutive — the pack carries the community's top

unaccountable veto); DO_NOT_USE is excluded from packs while USE_WITH_CARE stays packable with its
reason travelling into every output. Edit suggestions have no admin path at all — the answer's author
decides. Every one of the four pack outputs carries "Community-rated answers, not official positions."

## LEX — STATUTORY CONSEQUENCES: THE COUNT IS THE SCALE, THE CLASSIFICATION IS THE WORK (2026-08-27 11:58 UTC)

Executes `docs/BRIEF_STATUTORY_CONSEQUENCES.md`. Full report:
`docs/LEX_STATUTORY_CONSEQUENCES_REPORT.md`.

The fifth Deepening pass is built, wired and driven live. ⚠⚠ **Charlie's question is answered
with real numbers: repealing the Equality Act does NOT mean 1,868 consequential amendments.**
CRaG 2010's 149 provision-level references classify as **92 no-action, 44 replace, 13
amendment-related** — some are dead letters, some need a substitute reference, most are
untouched.

### ⚠⚠ §5'S SUGGESTED CAVEAT IS FALSE, AND IT WOULD HAVE MISLED EVERY USER

The brief offers: *"It does not yet cover statutory instruments — the regulations made under
Acts."* **SIs are the LARGEST source type in the graph: 793,616 of 1,034,548 rows, and 1,347
of the Equality Act's 1,868 references come FROM SIs.** A user shown that sentence would be
told we cannot see the layer supplying **72%** of their answer. What IS missing is the
**made-under** relationship — a different and stronger fact — which the `enabling-power`
layer reports as not-built from its own live count. ⚠ **This is the case FOR the computed
rule, not against the brief**: a hand-written caveat was wrong within a fortnight of a layer
landing; a queried one cannot be.

### ⚠⚠ A THIRD OF `citation_text` IS LEAKED XML, NOT THE SOURCE'S WORDS

**334,740 of 1,034,548 rows (32.4%)** carry XML attributes — `IdURI="…"
NumberOfProvisions="3"> Citation 1 This Order may be cited as…`; 34.9% of CRaG's
provision-level rows. It matters more here than anywhere else because §3 requires every
disposition to be **traceable to those words**, and a quotation that renders as XML soup
looks like a bug and teaches the reader to distrust the panel. Cleaned at read time, and what
cannot be cleaned is **counted, never dropped**: *"150 of the 1,552 have no quotable words."*
⚠ **Reported upstream rather than fixed** — the extractor owns the column and repairing it in
one consumer leaves every other consumer wrong.

### ⚠ `inbound()` CANNOT BE CALLED FROM THE WEB APP — the brief assumed it could

It lives in `scripts/ingest/graph/`; §20 check 0 forbids a file outside `scrutinise-web` from
entering the web program (a cross-package import caused a two-day outage on ~22 Aug), and it
reaches for `fs` and a 4GB zip that does not exist on a serverless filesystem. The TABLE is
reachable — same Neon database. So `lib/lex/statutory-graph.ts` is a **second reader of one
table**: a drift risk not removed, only made LOUD by `verify:statutory-parity`, which runs
both readers and fails on disagreement. ⚠ **It found a real gap on its first run** — the
`amendment-effects` layer was missing, the one this feature can least afford to lose
(*"a repeal or an amendment is not a citation and is not returned by this query"*). Parity now
holds row-for-row: CRaG 182/182, Equality Act 1,868/1,868.

### ⚠ THE INDEX DEFEAT, AND WHY THE OBVIOUS FIX WOULD HAVE BEEN WRONG

`WHERE lower(target_act_id) = $1` defeats `citation_edge_target_act`: **parallel seq scan over
1,034,548 rows at 474ms against 3.7ms on the index — 127×**. ⚠ But dropping `lower()` naively
would have been wrong in the direction that matters: **3,531 rows (0.34%) are not lower-case
— the pre-1963 regnal-year Acts** (`ukpga/Eliz2/9-10/33`, `ukpga/Vict/24-25/100`), i.e.
exactly the old heavily-referenced statutes a repeal programme touches. Measured before
choosing: **no Act id is stored in more than one casing**, so equality against both candidate
forms is complete AND indexable. End to end **25,005ms → 4,771ms**, identical results.

### §6 — THE COST, MEASURED

⚠⚠ **The large target costs the same as the small one**: 1,552 references and 149 both produce
**6 groups and ONE model call** (2,337ms vs 2,315ms), because classification runs over KINDS
and never over references. **Measured cost of a wired run, re-read from `LlmSpend`: 0.1007p**
— about **1.5% of a ~6.8p build. It does not double a build's cost.** §6 said report the
figure and do not choose; the include-always-or-on-request decision is Charlie's.

### §1 — the mechanism's own test met, and check:deepening fired three times correctly

A `PASSES` entry plus a job; no new route, component or engine branch. ⚠ **No search intents,
deliberately** — it reads a graph, and intents would run a keyword search and file the result
beside verified references, which §7 forbids. The guard fired on: **the job key and pass key
being the same string** (two registries sharing one name are indistinguishable to a source
guard and to a reader — now `CITATION_CONSEQUENCES`); the hardcoded **four-pass count**; and
**"every pass must declare intents"** — whose real invariant is *a pass must be able to
retrieve*, so it now accepts intents OR jobs. ⚠ **As written it would have forced the defect.**
`jobQuestion` was a two-way ternary that would have silently handed a third job the devolution
question; now a `Record<JobKey, string>` where omission is a compile error.

### Verified, and watched failing

`check:statutory` **17 passed, 7 with negative controls**, all watched rejecting — including
§8's required *"a check fails if any coverage wording is a literal"*. `check:deepening` all
pass; 25a 40, 25b 54, 25c 32, 25d 77, 25e 28, 25f 62, 25g 27, 25h 20, 25i 14. `tsc`,
`next build`, clean-build `--fast` clean (0 cross-package files).
⚠ **`check:statutory` failed twice on its first runs and both defects were in the check** —
the figure guard matched a TEMPLATE LITERAL CONTAINING CODE and reported an array index as a
corpus figure, then an unterminated backtick let a match span half the file. **A guard for
prose has to know what prose looks like**, or the next person to hit a false positive deletes
it.

### ▶ Carried to Search/Graph, reported as sent, no files of theirs edited

(1) the cross-reference graph should be **its own listed graph** in `SEARCH_STRATEGY` §9, not
folded into the citation/amendment row; (2) **the 32.4% XML-in-`citation_text` defect** above.

## CENTRAL Stage 2h items 6–8 — colour is never the only cue, and the frame that was wired to one surface (2026-08-27 08:41 UTC)

Closes the 2h brief. `npm run check:central` **693/693** (was 620), `next build` clean.

### ⚠⚠ The defect Charlie found in the browser: the approval frame was wired to Resources only

He reported the checkbox and the flag UI working and **no bold or colour framing** on "Approved by
Reform UK". Correct: the answer card rendered `ApprovalLabel` and `ApprovalCheckbox` and **never
`ApprovalFrame`**. The 2px border and the top-right superscript existed in the component and were
used by the resources grid alone, so an approved answer was indistinguishable from an unapproved one
on the surface that matters most.

**⚠ My own check did not catch it, and the reason is the third instance of one shape this sprint.**
It grepped `components/central/ApprovalFrame.tsx` for `borderWidth: 2` and for the superscript
string. That proves the component **can** draw a frame; it cannot notice a surface that imports the
label and not the frame. **A component test is not a surface test.** The check now asserts, per
surface, that the frame, the tick and the Context note are each rendered — watched failing by
renaming the tag.

`ApprovalFrame` gained `chrome={false}` for callers that already draw the card: `.central-card` and
`rounded-xl border border-border` are both single-class selectors, so which 1px border wins is
decided by stylesheet order rather than by intent.

### Item 8 — "Awaiting {Organisation} approval"

Was "Not approved material", which states a **verdict** about the content. "Awaiting" states a
position in a process. Most material is simply unmarked, and the neutral default must not read as a
judgement that somebody looked and declined.

### Item 6 — no state in Central is signalled by colour alone

Charlie is colour blind, so a voted state that differs from an unvoted one only by teal-versus-grey
means he cannot tell whether his own click registered. **⚠ `aria-pressed` was already on every one of
these controls and does not help** — it speaks to a screen reader, not to a sighted person who cannot
separate two hues. The second cue has to be visual.

`lib/state-cues.ts` is one vocabulary so five controls cannot invent five answers:

1. **Shape** — a solid glyph on, a hollow glyph off (▲/△, ▼/▽). **Four different characters, not one
   character recoloured**: survives greyscale, every form of colour blindness, and a photocopier.
2. **Weight** — `border-2` and bolder type, the same 2px the approval frame uses.

**Changed (five controls, all hue-only):** the question vote in the library list, the question vote
on the detail header, the answer vote, the resource vote, and the resource type chips — whose 7%
tint and `font-medium` was not a cue anybody could see.

**Found already carrying a second cue and left alone:** flags (the level is the badge text), role
badges (the role is the text), the AI label, the approval stamp, favourites (★/☆), context chips and
leaderboard tabs (a filled background against a white one is a **lightness** difference, which colour
blindness preserves), bulletin votes (`strokeWidth` 3 vs 2), and the leaderboard delta — red/green is
the classic deuteranopia pair, but it prints a leading `+` or `−`, and the sign is the cue.

**⚠ Two findings came from the check rather than from reading the code.** The platform's own accent
text `--central-teal-text: #0f8b7f` scores **4.18:1** on white — below the WCAG AA floor of 4.5 for
body text — and had never been measured. Now `#0d7a6f` at 5.21, same hue. And a **second
question-vote control**, on the question detail header, that the first sweep missed: the guard
asserts the **absence of a bare triangle** rather than the presence of a fix, which is exactly why it
found the one I did not know about.

### Item 7 — a per-user platform accent

**Reason on record:** Central's live-state accent is a teal close to one party's brand colour, which
is a poor look for a neutral platform whichever party it resembles. Letting each person choose
removes the question rather than answering it.

**⚠ A fixed palette, not a picker.** Free hex entry produces unreadable and non-compliant
combinations within about four clicks. Seven entries, each with its three values **hand-set rather
than derived** — deriving text colours from a base by a fixed lightness shift is precisely what
generates the unreadable combinations the palette exists to avoid: a mid-yellow darkened by a fixed
amount is still unreadable, and a mid-blue darkened by the same amount is nearly black.

**⚠ `check:central` computes WCAG contrast for every entry and fails below 4.5:1** — that is what
"pre-vetted" has to mean, or the word is decoration. A palette that has never been measured is the
same problem free hex was rejected for, arrived at more slowly. It is what caught the platform teal.

The column stores the palette **key**, not a hex: a hex column is a free-hex feature with extra
steps, since any future route could write anything to it. `NULL` means "never chosen", kept
distinguishable from "chose the default", so a future change to the platform default follows
everyone who never expressed a preference. Teal stays first and stays the default.

**⚠ Applied by a CLIENT component, and that is the design rather than a shortcut.** Reading the
accent in the root layout would opt the **entire app** — including the static signed-out marketing
pages — into dynamic rendering, to deliver a cosmetic preference only signed-in members have. The
`localStorage` cache is what stops the flash; nothing depends on it, and every access is wrapped
because in some contexts the accessor itself throws rather than returning null.

The check asserts the override set **matches the tokens `globals.css` declares exactly**. A ninth
token added to the stylesheet and not to the palette would leave one value stuck on the old teal for
everyone who chose another colour — a half-applied accent, which shows up on one surface nobody
thinks to check. Watched failing by adding a ninth token.

The picker labels each swatch **by name** (item 6): a row of coloured circles is a control a
colour-blind member cannot read at all, and this is the one screen where that would be absurd.

### Two guards that were narrower than the property they guarded

**⚠ The bare-triangle guard.** First version looked for a glyph in quotes or directly between `>` and
`<`. A planted bare ▲ dropped into JSX text after a comment went straight past it. Assert the
absence **totally** — and route even the explanatory hint copy through the vocabulary, so the hint
cannot drift from the control it describes.

**⚠ An assertion that was `[]` against `[]`.** The `globals.css` token comparison sliced from the
first `:root {` — and the file has **two**, with the accent tokens in the second. It compared an
empty list to an empty list and passed; it was caught only because the other side was non-empty once
the palette existed. Scanning the whole file is both simpler and correct.

### Audit of the rest of the 2h brief — already built, re-verified in code

Items 1–5 were all present: the invite normalisation with one validator on both paths; the topic
taxonomy (19 + 3, departments dropped, root-only, no "Other", Untagged view, per-topic counts); the
fractional referral accrual; all four training-UI items; the primary Choose File button with "File
selected"; and the vote hint. Reported rather than rebuilt, per the brief's instruction.

## CENTRAL Stage 2g + items 12–15 — resources, whose approval it is, and the empty block a video answer printed (2026-08-27 04:39 UTC)

Executes Stage 2g and items 12–15 of the 2g brief. `npm run check:central` **620/620** (was 472),
`next build` clean, 148 new assertions, four planted-break batches watched failing.

### Stage 2g — the Resources library

`Resource` + `ResourceVote` / `ResourceFlag` / `ResourceReport`, nine types, card grid with
thumbnails, type chips primary and topic dropdown secondary, top/newest sort. Voting is the answer
vote — up/down, one per member, no self-voting, same tariffs, same ledger — and AI-authored material
ranks and mints nothing, exactly as an answer does. Delete and restore are the 2f content pattern
unchanged, so a removed resource reverses its points and comes back with them.

**⚠ The upload gate is an allow-list checked against the SNIFFED BYTES, not a block-list checked
against the declared type.** "No executables or archives" written as a deny-list is `.exe`, `.scr`,
`.bat`, `.zip`, `.7z`, `.iso`, `.jar`, `.msi`, `.dmg`, `.apk` and whatever next year invents; and a
client can declare any MIME it likes, so renaming `setup.exe` to `poster.png` changes the
declaration and not the bytes. Images and PDFs only, magic-byte matched, 10 MB cap, and the file is
gated **before R2 sees it** — checking after storing means the rejected executable was already
written and reachable by key for as long as the cleanup took. Video and websites are links only, per
the standing decision; nothing is hosted, transcoded or proxied.

The copyright confirmation is a **hard gate recorded against the row** (`rightsConfirmedByUserId`,
`rightsConfirmedAt`), not a checkbox that vanishes on submit — without it the platform is hosting
other people's material on nobody's word. Report is on every resource for **every member**, not just
managers: it is the copyright escalation route, and the person who recognises their own work is
exactly the person with no rights over the Community that posted it.

### Item 12 — Community settings, and the colour that could not carry the meaning

Root-only settings: organisation name, colour, approval show/hide, four approval modes (default
SELF). Reform Branch Community seeded with Reform UK / `#17B9D1`. Generic platform machinery —
nothing party-specific is hard-coded anywhere; a second Community sets its own without a deploy.

**⚠ The brief asked for the colour to be checked against the platform's teal, and it failed the
check.** `#17B9D1` against `#14b8a6` measures **ΔE2000 15.14, hue gap 15°** — plainly different side
by side, and indistinguishable at the size a 1px border and a 10px superscript actually render. So
the frame is distinguished by **border weight (2px, which no platform accent uses) and its words**,
with colour as reinforcement only. A party stamp that read as a platform live-state would have the
platform vouching for material it has never seen.

### Item 13 — the name is always shown, and hiding is not deletion

**⚠ The stamp reads "{Organisation} approved — marked by {name}" in EVERY mode, without exception.**
Under the default mode the tick is the poster's own claim about their own material; rendering an
unverified self-tick as a bare organisational endorsement puts the organisation's name on something
it has never seen.

Hiding the feature removes the name, the frame and the superscript and **retains every row** —
`approvedAt`/`approvedByUserId` are untouched, and re-enabling restores exactly what was there.
Watched: the check approves an item, hides the feature, asserts the stamp stops rendering, asserts
the column is still populated, and re-enables to get the same name back.

A `Do not use` flag takes **visual precedence** over an approval and the two **coexist in the data**
— one person's approval does not clear another's flag, and the reader must never see an
organisation's endorsement as the loudest thing on an item an admin has told them not to use.

The Context box is **permanent** and unaffected by the toggle, with an HTML placeholder rather than
pre-filled content: pre-filled text is submitted verbatim by everyone who ignores it, and the
library fills with rows that literally read "When / Where / How to be used".

**⚠ One rule, two callers.** `lib/approval.ts` imports prisma, so a client control cannot call it,
and the obvious shortcut is to re-express "who may approve" in the component — after which the tick
appears for people the route refuses, or hides from people it allows, silently either way. The four
modes now live in `lib/approval-rule.ts` as one pure function that both the route gate and the
client control call.

### Item 14 — the empty block

An Answer may carry an external video URL instead of, or alongside, body text. **⚠ A video answer
has an EMPTY body**, so every surface that renders `answer.body` directly prints a blank where an
answer should be — the library preview, the collapsed detail row, and all four pack formats. One
function, `answerDisplayText`, turns an answer into what a text-only surface prints, and all four
formats plus the library list now call it: "a video answer prints as its title plus the URL, never
as an empty block" is one assertion rather than four, and a fifth format added later inherits it
instead of forgetting it. The A4 sheet deliberately prints the URL in full rather than linking it,
because paper is paper. The submit guard was also `!body.trim()`, which silently swallowed a
link-only answer.

### Item 15 — the three tab headings

Questions, Resources and Training carry their standing descriptions verbatim, grepped by the check
with whitespace collapsed, because JSX wraps the sentences across lines. Tab order is now
Questions · Training · Resources · Leaderboard · Teams, asserted by index order rather than by eye.

### ⚠⚠ Two partial indexes had been added WITHOUT a §21 register row, and nothing said so

`Community_live_children_idx` (item 11, yesterday) and `Resource_live_idx` (this sprint) were both
created in hand-written SQL and neither appeared in the hazard register. They were found by sweeping
`pg_indexes` by hand, not by any check — **because the §21 rule-5 assertion named two indexes
literally and had never been widened.** A register whose completeness check covers a quarter of it
is the failure mode §21 exists to prevent.

Both are now registered (eight entries), both models carry the `⚠` doc comment §21 rule 3 requires,
and the check now (a) enumerates every guarded index, asserting existence, predicate and register
row, and (b) sweeps `pg_indexes` for any partial index on a Central table that is **missing** from
the register — so the next omission fails a check instead of waiting for a sweep. Watched failing:
deleting the `Resource_live_idx` row turns both red, and the sweep names the offender.

### Watched failing

Four planted-break batches, each reverted:

- **upload + video + heading** — 12 red: every upload refusal, every `answerDisplayText` case, the
  library preview, the pack, and the Questions description.
- **approval** — 5 red: the feature flag beating the mode, the rights gate, the marked-by name, the
  control being offered while hidden, and re-enable restoring.
- **ledger + precedence** — the resource ledger reversal, the restore, and the 2px frame.
- **register** — the enumeration and the sweep.

**⚠ One planted break found a check that was testing the wrong guard.** Removing the no-self-voting
check from `applyResourceVote` left "you cannot vote on your own resource" **green**, because
`assertCanMark` also refuses self-marking and says "your own post" — the assertion was
`.includes('your own')` and was reading the backstop. It now asserts the exact wording, plus a
second case on an **AI-authored** resource, where nothing is minted so `assertCanMark` never runs at
all and the resource-level guard is the only thing there.

Also fixed en route: the deleted-items view could not render a `resource` kind; a Neon connection
drop mid-run left orphaned `zz-check-*` fixtures that the next run reported as failures (swept).

## SEARCH S15-CAPACITY — THE FOUR HYPOTHESES ANSWERED, AND THE FIRST REAL FOUR-STREAM BASELINE (2026-08-27 10:44 UTC)

Executes `docs/BRIEF_SEARCH_S15_CAPACITY.md`, which supersedes the earlier S15 draft. §§2, 3, 5 and
7 were delivered against that draft at 04:12 UTC; what follows is what the capacity brief added.

**§1 — the four hypotheses, with predictions logged at 10:30 before any was tested. Two of the
three predictions were wrong, and the wrong ones were worth more than the right one.**

| | verdict | the number |
|---|---|---|
| **H1** arbitrary constant | ✅ TRUE | `VECTOR_MAX_CONCURRENT ?? '4'`, copied from `fts-query-service.ts` |
| **H2** processor-bound | ⚠ PARTLY | the container has **8 vCPU**, not the 48 `os.cpus()` reports; width 16 burns **4.1–4.6** of them |
| **H3** memory-bound | ❌ FALSE | 1.95 GB of an 8 GB limit — but the index is **147.58 GB**, and I predicted 2–8 |
| **H4** storage/network | ✅ TRUE, DOMINANT | 193 GB in R2, **no local cache**, `cpu/wall 0.53` on a quiet query |

⚠⚠ **`os.cpus()` ON RAILWAY REPORTS THE HOST, NOT THE CGROUP QUOTA.** The 04:12 draft of this report
printed "a host reporting 48 cores" as evidence of headroom; the real limit is **8**, read from
Railway's `CPU_LIMIT`. That was an inference in the grammar of a measurement (§19) and it is the
most consequential correction here, because it is the number every future width decision rests on —
and it retro-explains the width-32 result the earlier draft could only call "confounded by drift":
at 4.1–4.6 of 8 vCPU, doubling the width would run into the quota.

⚠⚠ **H3's size prediction was wrong by more than twenty times, and the reason is the finding.**
Predicted 2–8 GB on the reasoning that IVF_PQ compresses 3,072 bytes per vector to ~96–192.
Measured: `corpus_vec.lance` is **147.58 GB** — `data` 130.55, `_indices` 16.92 — or **6,990 bytes
per vector, 2.3× LARGER than raw f32, not smaller.** Both halves of the reasoning were true and
combined wrongly: the PQ compression is real but lives **only** in `_indices` (746 bytes/vector, a
genuine 4.1×), while `data` keeps the original vectors AND the string columns. ⚠ And that matters
per query, because **`refineFactor: 2` re-ranks with EXACT distance and so must fetch original f32
vectors out of the 130 GB `data` directory** — ~1.8 MB per query on top of the `nprobes: 64`
partition reads. Also named: **`corpus_chunks/_versions` is 13.39 GB of stale manifests**, 29% of
that dataset, serving no query.

⚠ **What could NOT be measured, stated rather than glossed: bytes per query.** Railway's
`NETWORK_RX_GB` did not move across a controlled 20-query window. H4 rests on four converging
indirect lines (no cache in code; `cpu/wall` 0.53; a ten-fold warm-up curve; the same code taking
130 s from a laptop for what the container does in ~2 s) and is stated as indicated, not measured.
**H4's fix — co-location on a Railway volume — is costed at ~$31/month for 193 GB, inside the
brief's $50 threshold, and deliberately NOT done: D-8.**

**§6 — THE BASELINE RETAKEN, AND IT IS THE FIRST NON-DEGRADED FOUR-STREAM MEASUREMENT THIS PROJECT
HAS EVER HAD.** `degraded: []`, `fully-configured`, `vector+209` engagement, index stamps matched.
⚠ S14's surviving artefact is named **`s14-arms-bm25.json`** and records `streams=NONE …
DEGRADED(1)` — its published recall figures describe a **keyword-only** system.

| | S13 (1 dense stream) | S14 (dense OFF) | **S15 (4 streams, arriving)** |
|---|---|---|---|
| in-stream@20 — what retrieval finds | 27/64 | 19/64 | **32/64 (50%)** |
| merged@20, round-robin — production today | 15/64 | 14/64 | **19/64 (30%)** |
| merged@20, judged + reranker | — | 19/64 | **30/64 (47%)** |
| @5, judged + reranker | — | 15/64 | **26/64 (41%)** |

**Both S13 and S14 are VOID as statements about production retrieval, for opposite reasons.**
▶ **Dense retrieval is worth THIRTEEN points of in-stream recall (19 → 32); S14 predicted "roughly
twelve".** My own predictions, logged before the run: in-stream@20 **24–32 → actual 32**; arm A
**18–24 → actual 19**; dense observed to arrive; rejection rate 0. All four held.

⚠⚠ **AND THE SENTENCE THAT SHOULD BE READ BEFORE ANY OF IT: with today's production configuration,
45 of 64 questions return nothing correct. With the judged merge and reranker on, 34 of 64. And a
PERFECT merge could only reach 32 of 64, because for half the set retrieval finds nothing at all.
The merge is no longer the constraint; retrieval is.** `debates` is **0/11** on every arm;
`committees` **2/10**; `impact-assessments` finds 4/9 and displays **0/9**.

**§3's acceptance measure — the rejection rate — is ZERO on every real workload**: 40 legs at two
users, 64 at four, 96 at eight, and **209 across the whole gold sweep**. Non-zero only when
`check-vector-shed` deliberately overfills the queue (6 of 54, by design), which is the shed path
proving it still works.

▶ **The clearest proof the capacity work landed: the gold harness no longer needs its throttle.**
`s14-run.sh` had to run at `LEX_STREAM_CONCURRENCY=1` and a 90 s timeout — its own comment says
that was "what makes the measurement possible at all". `s15-run.sh` uses production's 3 and 25 s
and completed with 0 rejections. ⚠ `LEX_STREAM_CONCURRENCY=3`'s stated justification ("under the
service's 4") is now void, but a void reason is not evidence for a new number — **D-7, measure it,
do not raise it blind.**

**Total spend: €0.008 (the index rebuild) + 13.68p (the reranker arms over 64 questions).**

## SEARCH S15-CAPACITY — PREDICTIONS FOR H2, H3 AND H4, LOGGED BEFORE ANY OF THEM WAS TESTED (2026-08-27 10:30 UTC)

Executes `docs/BRIEF_SEARCH_S15_CAPACITY.md` §1, which requires a prediction per hypothesis
recorded before testing. Written before the index size, the compression parameters, the
per-query byte count or the CPU utilisation had been read.

⚠ **H1 is NOT predicted here because it is already answered** (earlier S15 draft, 04:12 UTC):
`vector-query-service.ts:86` is `parseInt(process.env.VECTOR_MAX_CONCURRENT ?? '4', 10)` — a plain
constant, copied from `fts-query-service.ts`'s `FTS_MAX_CONCURRENT`, whose justifying measurement
was taken on the FTS service. Predicting a thing already measured would be scoring myself on a
known answer.

**H2 — processor-bound. Predicted FALSE as the primary constraint.**
- CPU during ONE isolated query will be **under 3 cores' worth sustained** (`cpu/wall < 3.0`).
- The container will report a vCPU limit **far below** the 48 `os.cpus()` reports (that is the
  HOST, not our cgroup quota) — I predict a limit of **8 or fewer**.
- The dominant stage will be the ANN, not the embed and not response assembly.

**H3 — memory-bound. Predicted FALSE.**
- `corpus_vec` on disk will be **2–8 GB**, not the ~70 GB the brief's uncompressed arithmetic
  gives, because the index is **IVF_PQ** — product-quantised, so a 768-dim float32 vector
  (3,072 bytes) is stored as roughly **96–192 bytes** plus overhead.
- The working set will **not** fit in the process's resident memory and **will not need to**:
  peak RSS is 1,773 MB against a 7,629 MB cap (23%), so nothing is paging.
- Adding RAM will therefore buy **nothing**.

**H4 — storage/network-bound. Predicted TRUE, and the primary constraint.**
- `lance.ts` opens both tables at `s3://{bucket}/_search` with **no local cache directory**, so
  every query is HTTP range reads against Cloudflare R2 from Railway `europe-west4`.
- Bytes read per dense query will be **more than 10 MB**, essentially all of it from object
  storage rather than local disk.
- This is consistent with the already-measured `cpu_over_wall` of **0.53** on a quiet service.

⚠ **The consequence if H4 is right is the expensive one:** more processor and more RAM both buy
nothing, replicas MULTIPLY the dominant cost because each re-reads R2 independently, and the fix
is to co-locate the index with the service — which is a different and larger change than any
capacity dial.

**Scored in `docs/SEARCH_S15_REPORT.md` §1.**

### And a second prediction, for §6.2's baseline retake (2026-08-27 10:47 UTC)

⚠ **Logged with the run already in flight and its output DELIBERATELY UNREAD** — the harness was
started before I had worked out what the retake actually measures, and a prediction written after
reading the answer is worthless. Stated here rather than quietly dropped.

**What the retake is, and why it is not a re-run of S14.** S14's headline
**in-stream@20 = 19/64 (30%)** was taken while **every dense leg was timing out and silently

**27–28/64 (42%)** was taken with dense on `legislation` ALONE. So there has never been a

the first time, and S14 sized the unmeasured gap at "roughly twelve points".

**Predicted:**
- **in-stream@20 lands between 24 and 32 of 64**, i.e. at or above S13's 27 — three more streams

## SEARCH S15 — THE SERVICE WAS NOT SLOW BECAUSE IT WAS FOUR WIDE (2026-08-27 04:12 UTC)

Executes `docs/BRIEF_SEARCH_S15.md`. Full report: `docs/SEARCH_S15_REPORT.md`.

**§0 — the audit changed the brief.** The brief's order was cancel → shed → batch → width. §1 found a
step nobody had costed: **1,478,964 rows of `corpus_chunks` (6.5% of 22,670,808) had fallen outside
its `sectionId` BTree index**, and every snippet lookup brute-force scanned them. Measured against
the live dataset: an equality lookup on the **indexed** column took **133,401 ms**, while the same
table's **unindexed** `chunkId` column answered in **21,470 ms** — the indexed column six times
slower than the unindexed one — against an ANN of **1,301 ms**. Independently corroborated on the
bill: `vector-serve` shows **NETWORK_RX_GB 3,168.5** month-to-date, ~3.17 TB of ingress for on the
order of a thousand queries.

⚠⚠ **The repository predicted it in writing and the check could not fail.**
`build-chunks-scalar-index.ts` carries the warning in its own header — *"THIS INDEX WILL NEED
REBUILDING IF THE MAX_CHUNKS TOP-UP HAPPENS … an append leaves new rows outside the index"* — and its
`--verify-only` asked *"is there an index on this column?"*, which an index missing 6.5% of the table
answers **yes**. It printed **"an index on sectionId EXISTS. Nothing to do."** It now reads
`indexStats()` and exits 4 on uncovered rows, with unreadable coverage treated as UNKNOWN rather than
as covered. Watched firing against the real stale state before it was trusted.

**The rebuild: 45.1 s, peak 1.82 GB, €0.008, box destroyed in a `finally`.** 22,670,808 indexed, 0
unindexed. Effect, with the ANN as the control because the rebuild touched only the chunks index:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| snippet stage | 3,296 ms (61%) | **1,233 ms (36%)** |
| ANN (control — should not move) | 1,889 ms | 1,934 ms |
| total service time | 5,421 ms | **3,394 ms** |
| peak RSS under an 18-request load | **5,586 MB (73.2% of cap)** | **1,253 MB (16.4%)** |

⚠ The memory result answers `fts-query-service.ts`'s open question of 7 Aug — *"this semaphore may be
guarding the wrong variable… the binding constraint is memory"* — from an unexpected direction: memory
**was** the real variable, and it was being spent on a stale index rather than on concurrency.

**§2 — cancellation, proven from outside, both ways.** Same script, same twelve requests, aborted at
t+2 s. Before: `served +12` after every client was dead, recovery **19 s**. After: `served +0`,
`abandoned +12`, recovery **3 s**; repeated at 48 requests, `served +0 · abandoned +48`, recovery
**6 s**. The measurement is the service's own `served` counter, which increments whether or not anyone
is on the socket — a latency could not distinguish *the queue drained* from *the queue was thrown
away*. Not even the four already running completed: they finished their ANN, met the between-stages
check, and were dropped before the expensive scan.

⚠ **Abandonment is counted per CACHE KEY, not per socket.** `QueryCache` coalesces concurrent
identical requests onto one `compute()`; cancelling on the owning socket alone would strand every
request behind it — a correctness bug introduced by a performance fix. `pump()` now skips abandoned
waiters instead of granting them a slot, which is where the queue actually drains.

**§3 — a bounded queue that says so.** Cap is `2 × width`, derived from the width so it tracks it
(64 on a 4-wide service promised the last caller sixteen service times). `check-vector-shed.ts`
**8/8**: 6 shed for 6 excess, **slowest refusal 420 ms** against the 25,000 ms client timeout it
replaces, every refusal machine-readable as `reason: 'overloaded'`, counted on `/stats`, and a
negative control at exactly-capacity that refuses nothing.

The refusal now reaches the gateway. `runVectorSearch` carries `overloaded` / `timeout` /
`unreachable` / `error` / `unscoped` instead of a bare `[]`; the router collects them per search
through `AsyncLocalStorage` (a module-level array would report one user's degradation inside
another's); the gateway surfaces `meta.denseDegraded`. **This closes S14 §0 at its source** — a
stream whose dense leg was refused used to return a ranking byte-for-byte identical to a stream that
never had one. `check:dense-degraded` **14/14**, every positive paired with the arrangement that must
not trigger it, **and it caught a real defect**: one entry's hydration throwing rejected the whole
`Promise.all` and turned a single stream's fault into a total batch failure — exactly what the brief
warned batching would do if written the obvious way.

⚠ `failed` is set only when the search returned **nothing** while a leg was refused. A partial gap
(BM25 ran, dense was shed) is recorded in `meta.denseDegraded` and `failed` stays false, because
saying *"I could not search the corpus"* while displaying twenty real documents is a false negative
about our own evidence. **This is a deliberate reading against the brief's literal wording and is
D-2.**

**§4 — refuted by its own measurement.** `POST /vector-search-batch` is built and live. Measured
against four concurrent solo requests, arms alternated: **batch 6,495 ms vs solo 2,873 ms — 126%
SLOWER**, because it serialises four ANNs inside one slot while four solo requests parallelise theirs
across four. The one-scan design did work (`snippetMs` 419–1,440 for all four streams together), but
after the index rebuild the scan is no longer the dominant stage. **Equivalence 20/20 stream-rounds,
id for id** — a pure transport change, so it can be wired in later without a retrieval regression.
**Not recommended.** `LEX_STREAM_CONCURRENCY` stays at 3, but its stated justification ("under the
service's 4") is now stale.

**§5 — width 4 → 16, and it cost nothing.** The 4 was a plain constant **copied from
`fts-query-service.ts`**, whose justifying measurement (10 concurrent = 226 s, 15 = crash) was taken
on the FTS service — and whose own note of 7 Aug records that it **did not reproduce here**: 64
concurrent ANN queries survived and throughput scaled ~4× from 1→8. Measured: at width 4, offering 8
bought only 12% over offering 4; at width 16, throughput **2.20 → 4.43 req/s** with the queue no
longer binding. One environment variable on the existing single replica; **no replicas added, memory
did not rise, £0.00**. `vector-serve-run.ts width <n>` reads the concurrency back **off the running
process** and refuses to report success if it disagrees — and that guard fired for real on its first
use before being made robust to the 502s a container swap produces.

⚠ Width 32 is **not** recommended but the evidence is weaker than I would like, and the report says
so: within one run it declined from offered 16 to 24, but the between-run absolute levels are
confounded by the service's known minute-to-minute drift, and two widths cannot be alternated inside
one process.

**§6 — the load test.** One user's search is four simultaneous stream-scoped requests.

| load | legs | ok | shed | timed out | per-stream p50 | queue HWM |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **2 users** | 40 | 40 | 0 | 0 | 3,276–3,728 ms | 0 |
| 4 users | 64 | 64 | 0 | 0 | 3,169–3,646 ms | 0 |
| 8 users | 96 | 96 | 0 | 0 | 4,307–5,881 ms | 16 of 32 |

Against S14, where **one** user saturated the service, all four dense streams returned at the 25 s
ceiling within 36 ms of each other, and `warm_p95` reached 706,954 ms still climbing forty minutes
after every client had been killed.

⚠⚠ **NOT DONE, AND IT IS THE LARGEST OMISSION: the 64-question recall baseline is not re-taken.**
Deliberate — this sprint changed latency and availability, not ranking, and re-running a three-hour
retrieval against services just reconfigured twice would attribute the reconfiguration to the
measurement. It is the next sprint's first job, and it is possible for the first time: S14's numbers
were taken while the dense legs were timing out and silently falling back to BM25, which is what
`meta.denseDegraded` now makes visible. Also not done: `fts-serve` still has an **unbounded queue**,
no cancellation, and the same copied width of 4.

**§7 — the deploy trap, hit and caught.** `vector-serve` has no repo trigger and does not auto-deploy;
it was found pinned to a **24 August** commit with 84 commits since (benign only because none touched
`scripts/ingest/search/`). `BUILD = 'S15-cancel-bounded-batch'` is now on `/health` and `/stats`,
false on every earlier build and true on this one, and `measure-vector-batch.ts` refuses to run
without it.

⚠ Git: three code commits mid-sprint, against §12's usual rule, because §7 makes a push the only way
to get code onto the service and nothing here could be verified without it. Scoped by explicit path.

**Total sprint spend: €0.008.** No Railway capacity purchased.

## LEX 25-I — THE DOCUMENT PIPELINE HAD NEVER RUN, AND THE REUSE CARRY DESTROYED THE RESEARCH IT REUSED (2026-08-27 03:09 UTC)

Executes `docs/BRIEF_25I.md`. Full report: `docs/LEX_25I_REPORT.md`.

The brief's instruction to **verify on the live site before changing anything** is what made
this sprint worth running: three of six sections found something different from what the
brief or 25-H believed, and two were defects invisible to any source grep.

### ⚠⚠ `IdeaUserMaterial` HAD ZERO ROWS IN THE ENTIRE PRODUCTION DATABASE

25-H reported §4 shipped, and the component IS real — file input, FormData, extraction,
findings pass. Nothing had ever been through it. Driving it with Charlie's own document
(*How is accountability measured…docx*, 40,877 bytes) found it **throwing away 73% of what it
read**: 15 findings offered, **11 dropped** as *"the quote could not be found in the
document"*. **Ten of the eleven quotes were in the document.** The eleventh shows the
mechanism — the model wrote `…over government. there` where the document has `…over
government there` — one added full stop. `quoteIsInText` is ALL-OR-NOTHING over the whole
passage, so one tidied character at position 200 discarded the entire finding, and told the
user their document had produced nothing. Same shape as the "fabrication rate" that was our
own undecoded HTML entities.

⚠ **THE FIX MAKES PROVENANCE STRONGER, NOT LOOSER.** Matching on the first few words or a
similarity score would admit a reconstruction — the thing the check exists to stop.
`verbatimSpan` finds the longest prefix of the model's quote that really is in the document
and stores **the document's own words for that span**; the model's string is never stored, so
a quote is verbatim BY CONSTRUCTION rather than by passing a test, and the floor rose 20 → 60
characters. **4 → 8 findings on the same document**; all 11 rejects now anchor; four negative
controls (invented; reworded at word 5; ten characters; under the floor) still refused.

### ⚠⚠ THE REUSE CARRY *MOVED* THE EVIDENCE, SO ONE ABORTED RE-RUN DESTROYED IT

25-G's `carryEvidenceForward` was an `updateMany` rewriting `runVersion` — a MOVE. It runs
inside `claimBuild`, **before a single pass**, so any re-run claimed and then failed,
cancelled or crashed took the previous build's research away permanently; the next re-run
reused from an empty source and died with *"the research pass produced nothing to revise
against"*. Measured live on Charlie's idea: **69 evidence rows stranded on a CANCELLED v2
that ran ZERO passes**, v1 left with 9 of its 78, v3 FAILED. One aborted re-run lost the whole
of a build he had paid for and nothing said so. ⚠ `runVersion` must be a fact about that
version; moving made it mean "the newest run interested in this row", and v1's screen would
go blank the moment anyone clicked Re-run. **It now COPIES.** Rows restored (v1 back to 78,
each count re-read); the restore targets only builds with **zero** passes, because a build
that failed at pass 5 legitimately owns what it read.

### §1 — loading a page created an idea

`BuildIdeaClient`'s boot POSTed `/api/ideas` on mount — not to record intent but because it
had no way to draw the first question without a row. ⚠ **25-E's resume made this LESS VISIBLE
without fixing it**: minting only happened to users whose rows were all empty or all built, so
it kept happening and stopped being obvious. *Resume is not creation control.*
`blankElicitationState()` now projects the first question from a blank row through **the same

## CENTRAL — the content soft-delete pattern, which item 11 will match (2026-08-26 23:32 UTC)

Charlie's call: build the content pattern first, then branch delete/restore on top of it. This is the
pattern. ⚠ **Whatever is wrong here is wrong in three more places by the end of the sprint**, which is
why it is one module — `lib/content-deletion.ts` — rather than a habit repeated per entity.

### Four columns, and what each is load-bearing for

`deletedAt` · `deletedByUserId` · `deletionReason` · `deletedWithParent`, on **Question**,
**Answer** and **BulletinPost**.

⚠ **`deletedWithParent` is the one that is easy to leave out and impossible to reconstruct later.**
Deleting a question takes its answers with it and stamps each as collateral. Restoring the question
must bring back exactly those and must NOT resurrect an answer its own author had deleted a week
earlier. Without the flag those two rows are identical and no amount of timestamp arithmetic recovers
the difference. It has its own assertion, and the planted break that flips it fails six checks.

⚠ **`Answer.hidden` is NOT this and stays.** Hidden is Stage 2b moderation — the answer exists, its
author still sees it, a manager has said "not this one" with a reason. Deleted is gone. Overloading
one for the other would make every later query about hidden answers silently include removed ones,
the same trap `idea_soft_delete.sql` recorded for `status='ARCHIVED'`. Asserted both ways: a
hidden answer is still visible to a manager who asks for hidden ones, a deleted one is not, even then.

### Points reverse at the value they were awarded

The ledger only ever appends. Deletion writes a negative event, restore writes the positive one back,
and both rows stay — award, reversal, restore is three rows and nothing is edited. Two new event
types, `CONTENT_DELETED` and `CONTENT_RESTORED`, distinct from `MARK_REMOVED` on purpose: that
one means the VOTER withdrew, these mean the content went away. Same effect on a total, different
cause, and an activity log that cannot tell them apart cannot explain why somebody's score moved.

⚠ **Summed from the ledger, not re-priced.** A mark may already have been withdrawn, in which case the
award and its `MARK_REMOVED` cancel and the net is zero — reversing each `MARK_RECEIVED`
individually would take points the author no longer has. Restore reads the deletion event back rather
than re-deriving the figure, so the two can never disagree, and a second restore is refused rather
than minting from nothing.

⚠ **One asymmetry, stated rather than hidden:** referral bonuses minted from an award are NOT clawed
back on deletion. That matches what `MARK_REMOVED` already does for a withdrawn mark. Doing it
differently here, while the withdrawn-mark path does something else, would be worse than the
asymmetry.

### A manager deleting somebody else's content must say why

Your own content needs no reason — nobody has to justify withdrawing their own words. Somebody else's
does, the same rule Stage 2e applied to reversing an activity claim, and the author is notified with
it. A plain member cannot remove another member's content at all.

### Deleted means invisible, asserted surface by surface

⚠ **A soft delete that one read forgets is worse than no delete at all**: the content is "removed" and
still on somebody's screen. The exclusion lives at the two chokepoints every read already flows
through — `getQuestionVisibilityFilter` and `getBoardScopeFilter` — rather than being remembered at
twenty call sites. Beyond those, the direct reads were found by enumerating them and fixed: ranked
answers, pack building, across-branches, the three topic views, the importer's idempotency (a deleted
question must not block a re-import of the same text), and both vote paths, so a stale tab cannot pay
points into content nobody can see.

Nine behavioural assertions call the real functions rather than trusting the filter, plus two greps as
a backstop for a surface nobody thought to assert.

### The deleted-items view

`/communities/[id]/deleted`, manage rights, cascading from every ancestor. ⚠ **Soft delete is only
half a feature without it**: `deletedAt` makes a removal reversible in principle, a list makes it
reversible in practice — otherwise "it's recoverable" means "recoverable by whoever can write SQL".
Cascaded rows are **included and labelled**: hiding them would make the counts lie, and offering to
restore one alone would put an answer back under a deleted question.

### Verified

`tsc --noEmit` and `next build` clean; **`npm run check:central` 436/436**, up from 387. **Six
planted breaks, all watched failing**: the cascade marker flipped, points not reversing, restore
re-pricing instead of reading the deletion back, and each of the two chokepoints losing its filter.

Three new partial indexes over the live rows are registered in `docs/CLAUDE.md` §21 — along with
`Idea_creatorId_live_idx`, which predates Central and **had been missing from the register since it
was written**.

▶ **Item 11 (branch delete/restore) is now unblocked** and is the next thing: same four columns on
`Community`, the same cascade marker onto branch-scoped questions and posts, the same points rule,
and the same deleted-items view — which is why the pattern went first.

## SURFACE — PRINCIPLE 7: THE APPLICATION'S CLAIM WAS FALSE, AND ITS PREMISE WAS WRONG TOO (2026-08-27 03:10 UTC)

Ran `docs/BRIEF_PRINCIPLE_7_VERIFY.md`. Evidence pack: `docs/PRINCIPLE_7_EVIDENCE.md`.

### What a search engine could see BEFORE — read off production, not off the repository

| checked on `www.scrutinise.org`, anonymously | before |
|---|---|
| `robots.txt` on the proposal pages | **`Allow: /ideas/`** |
| `<meta name="robots">` on a proposal page | **none** |
| `X-Robots-Tag` on any response | **none** |
| proposal page fetched as `GPTBot`, `ClaudeBot`, `CCBot`, `Bytespider` | **HTTP 200, the full 42 KB, each time** |
| rate limiting on those paths | **none** — 20 sequential and 10 concurrent all 200 |
| WAF / bot challenge | **none** — `server: Vercel`, nothing in front |

**So the draft application's statement — that judgment pages carry `noindex, nofollow` and that
`robots.txt` disallows those paths — was false in every part.**

### ⚠⚠ AND THE PREMISE WAS WRONG IN A WAY THAT MATTERED MORE

**There is no judgment page on this site, and there never was one to noindex.** Judgment text
reaches a reader only as a short extract inside a policy proposal, written by Lex from a retrieved
passage. So the surface principle 7 governs is the **proposal page** — which the product had
deliberately made public, listed in `robots.txt` as `Allow`, and which `sitemap.ts` was written to
advertise to Google as soon as any proposal reached Stage 4.

⚠ The sitemap was clean **by accident**: it produced 0 proposal entries only because no proposal has
reached Stage 4 yet. It would have started contradicting the noindex the day one did.

### What changed, and what it costs

**Every `/ideas` page is `noindex, nofollow` in three places** — the meta tag
(`app/ideas/layout.tsx` and the detail page), the `X-Robots-Tag` header (`next.config.js`, which
also covers the public JSON reads that have no HTML to put a tag in), and `robots.txt`. Three,
because a crawler may honour any one and ignore the others. **`robots.txt` now names 27 AI and
bulk-collection crawlers individually**, because a wildcard does not bind an agent that looks for
its own name. Proposal pages are removed from the sitemap.

⚠ **A per-proposal flag was considered and rejected by Charlie.** It would have kept proposals
discoverable by noindexing only the ones carrying a judgment extract — and the licence application
states this as a **fact**. A detector that silently stops firing turns a legal claim false with
nobody watching; a blanket rule cannot silently stop applying. **The cost was accepted: no proposal
page appears in any search engine.**

### Verified from outside, after the deploy — production serving `b093e89`

```
/ideas/be7d7b70-…   HTTP 200   X-Robots-Tag: noindex, nofollow, noarchive, nosnippet
                               <meta name="robots" content="noindex, nofollow, nocache"/>
/api/ideas/{id}/research       X-Robots-Tag: noindex, nofollow, noarchive, nosnippet
sitemap.xml                    25 entries, 0 under /ideas/
GPTBot · ClaudeBot · CCBot · Bytespider · PerplexityBot → all served the noindex header
CONTROL: / and /about          X-Robots-Tag: (none), no meta robots  ← still indexable
```

⚠ **The control is the load-bearing line.** A verification in which everything comes back `noindex`
cannot tell a targeted rule from a blanket one applied to the whole site.

### The rate limit fires, and it is reported as a speed bump rather than a control

120 requests per minute per hashed IP on the corpus-bearing paths, failing open. **Watched firing:
request 141 returned HTTP 429 with `Retry-After: 60`.** ⚠ It fired at 141 rather than 121 because
the counter lives in one edge instance's memory and the run spread across more than one — **which
is exactly the limitation, measured rather than assumed. A collector that spreads its requests gets
a fresh budget from each instance, and the application must not claim this prevents bulk
collection.**

### Q21 — "Will you make the entire record available online?"

**No.** Measured: an extract is **252 characters at the median, 776 at the longest**, against a
median stored case-law section of **~37,575 characters** — about **0.7% of one section**, and a
section is only part of a judgment. **74,896 of 74,896** case-law records carry their Find Case Law
URL. And today **0 of 135** evidence rows and **0 of 4** research rows carry any judgment text at
all.

⚠ **Still open and named in the evidence pack:** the definitive index check is Google Search
Console, which cannot be read from this machine (§19) — Charlie can settle it in a minute, and the
number belongs in the pack before submission. There is no WAF. And a `Disallow` stops a
well-behaved crawler ever seeing the `noindex`, which is the right order only while nothing is
indexed.

⚠ **Nothing here touches retrieval.** Lex's search over the corpus — the licensed activity — is
server-side against `fts-serve`/`vector-serve` and reads no robots directive of ours.

## CENTRAL — filling the template for a real branch found two faults in it (2026-08-26 15:08 UTC)

Charlie asked for the Q&A in `docs/ReformUK_Harrogate_Two_Sheet_WITH_EVIDENCE.pdf` put into the
upload template, ready to hand to a branch chair. **Doing it end to end is what surfaced both faults
below — neither was visible from reading the code.**

### The file

`docs/ReformUK_Harrogate_Questions_UPLOAD.xlsx` — 13 questions, 13 answers, 0 errors against the
real importer. Built by editing the shipped template's XML **in place**: `styles.xml`,
`theme1.xml`, the "Read me first" and "Valid values" sheets and `workbook.xml` all come out
**byte-identical**, 12 zip entries in and 12 out, and the Context drop-down survives on `B3:B205` —
data starts at row 3 precisely so every Context cell is inside it.

⚠ **The source is not a Q&A document.** It is a persuasion sheet organised by topic plus a training
sheet, so eleven of the thirteen questions had to be WRITTEN from the script each one answers. Only
three are verbatim — the objection lines *"That seems harsh"*, *"We need renewables"* and *"We should
help migrants"*. Every inferred row says so in its Notes column, which is never imported.

### Fault 1 — a comma is not a separator, and could not be

`splitList` treated commas, semicolons and newlines alike. **Five of the thirty-five topics the
shipped template offers in its own "Valid values" list contain commas** — Department for Culture,
Media and Sport; Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs; Department for Science,
Innovation and Technology; Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office; Ministry of Housing,
Communities and Local Government. Picking DCMS from that list produced the tags **"Department for
Culture"** and **"Media and Sport"**: two junk topics, created silently. It shredded citation text in
Sources the same way.

The template has always said *"Separate several with a semicolon"*, so this is the parser being made
to match its own documentation. Someone who commas them anyway now gets one long unknown topic, which
the preview **shows** as a topic that would be created — visible and correctable rather than silent.
⚠ **I shipped those department names last sprint and did not try using one.** Filling in the template
for real is what found it.

### Fault 2 — a Community created after the migrations has no tags at all

Every tag in every Community came from a migration — `central_stage2b.sql` seeded the contexts and
six topics, 2d promoted five more, 2e added the departments — and each ran **once**, against the nodes
that existed then. Community creation seeded `bulletinCategories` and nothing else.

**Found because a branch created at 13:40 today turned `check:central` red**, which is the check
doing its job on data nobody wrote for it.

For a new BRANCH it was survivable: the library reads its ROOT's tags. **For a new top-level Community
it was not** — empty chip row, empty topic dropdown, and every row of a bulk upload failing with
*"… is not a context in this Community. Use one of:"* followed by an empty list. Directly on the path
Charlie described: *"once they've set up their branch"*.

Creation now seeds the set (`seedQuestionTags`, one source of truth in `lib/community.ts`), and
`scripts/backfill-question-tags.ts` is the catch-up — dry-run by default, idempotent. ✅ The starter
set is **43 tags**, which is exactly what all four pre-existing nodes already had, so it is the real
set rather than one invented for the occasion. The one node missing it, **Cramlington and
Killingworth**, has been seeded.

### Verified

`tsc --noEmit` and `next build` clean; **`npm run check:central` 377/377**, up from 372. New
coverage: a topic whose own NAME contains a comma survives the parser in one piece and is not reported
as two new topics; a comma-separated cell stays one visible unknown rather than half-working; and
every Community has a context tag set, because without one it can accept no upload at all.

## SEARCH S14 — THE MERGE STOPS RATIONING SLOTS; AND `vector-serve` CANNOT SERVE FOUR DENSE STREAMS (2026-08-26 14:45 UTC)

**Report:** `docs/SEARCH_S14_REPORT.md` · **Brief:** `docs/BRIEF_SEARCH_S14.md` · raw data
`docs/census/s14-score-audit.json`, `docs/census/s14-arms-bm25.json`.
**Index of record: `corpus_fts` v7308 / 18,272,377 rows** — stamped either side of every run, and
the same index S13 measured against.

▼ **§0 FIRST, BECAUSE IT IS THE ONLY THING HERE HAPPENING ON A RUNNING SERVICE.** `vector-serve`
runs **4 requests wide behind a 64-deep queue, and a client abort does not cancel work already
queued** — so a dense leg that times out at the 25 s client ceiling is still executed after the
caller has walked away. Every timeout therefore *adds* load rather than shedding it. Measured:
`inFlight 4 · queued 64/64 · rejections 101`, and `warm_p95` read off the same counter at four
points in one afternoon — **7,698 ms quiet → 205,754 → 351,301 → 706,954 ms**. ⚠⚠ **It kept
climbing for forty minutes after every client had been killed.** Every earlier measurement in this
project ran with `LEX_VECTOR_STREAMS=legislation` — ONE dense call per query. **Production reads
four.** The per-stream timings carry their own control: at width 20, the four dense-enabled streams
returned in **25,0xx ms** (the client timeout) on all three probes, to within 36 ms of each other,
while `debates` — the one stream with no dense leg — returned in **4.0–6.1 s**, nine times out of
nine. ⚠ It leaves no mark on the result: `mergeLegs` returns the BM25 list and every hit keeps
`scorer: 'bm25'`, byte-for-byte what a stream with no dense leg produces. **D-1.**

▶ **§1 — THE DURABLE FINDING, WRITTEN DOWN SO THE NEXT READER DOES NOT REBUILD IT: plain rank
fusion across streams IS round-robin.** The streams return disjoint sets — measured, **0 of 10
stream pairs shared a single document on any of three probes, 30 pairwise comparisons, 0 shared
ids** — and over disjoint sets unweighted RRF sorts by `1/(k+rank)`, which takes every stream's
rank 1, then every stream's rank 2. `check:s14-merge` §A asserts it by comparing outputs, not by
reading the code. **Rank fusion carries no information about whose rank 1 is better.** Scores do not
either: a caselaw rank-1 at **53.4** against a legislation rank-1 at **254.2**, with caselaw's BEST
below legislation's MEDIAN on every probe — and after fusion they are not even the same function.
Score normalisation is **REJECTED** for a specific reason: it rescales a stream relative to its own
candidates, so a stream that found nothing good is promoted to parity with one that found something
excellent.

▶ **§2 — `LEX_SEARCH_JUDGED_MERGE`, default OFF.** At least 20 retrieved per routed stream always
(`SEARCH_MIN_PER_STREAM`); the displayed twenty chosen by judgement over the whole pool; **one
source may hold all twenty.** Constructed case: round-robin gives the answering stream **4 of 20**
by construction, the judged merge **20 of 20**. Measured on the validated set over the 40 questions
routing 3+ streams: **the round-robin's mean maximum share is 5.4 and it never exceeds 7** — the
arithmetic ceiling, visible as a measurement. Every judged arm exceeds it. ⚠ The degenerate case is
today's behaviour **id for id** (floor 2, uniform weights, no gate = `interleaveStreams`), which is
what makes every arm attributable. ⚠ Nothing is ever dropped: the relevance gate DEMOTES and counts.
**`LEX_MERGE_COVERAGE` is DELETED, not defaulted off** — the signal survives in `term-coverage.ts`.

▶ **§5 — THE ARMS, n = 64, keyword-only and labelled as such** (§0 is why: with the production
string set, the run would have produced the same keyword-only rankings while claiming a dense
configuration). in-stream@20 **19/64** · round-robin **14/64** · confidence **14/64** · gate 11/64 ·
both 12/64 · **reranker 18/64 (pro) and 19/64 (flash) — which is in-stream@20 EXACTLY: everything
retrieval found is displayed — with @5 going 6/64 → 15/64.** ⚠⚠ **Against S13 on the same index,
dense retrieval was worth about TWELVE POINTS of in-stream recall** (42% → 30%) — a bigger number
than anything the merge does, which is why D-1 comes before D-2. **The deterministic arms are S13's
coverage arm again**: three quarters of rankings moved to buy nothing, with documents their own
stream ranked SECOND landing at merged **143** and **161**. The reranker arms are the only ones with
a different shape (+5/−1 and +6/−1), and every gain is a document deeper than floor(20/S) in its own
stream — in-stream 14, 16, 39, 47 — exactly the ones S13's arithmetic said could never be shown.
⚠ Its one loss is the shape to watch: a document its own stream ranked FIRST taken to merged 27.
**D-4: recommended ON, after D-1.**

▶ **§1(b) — ASK FOR A PERMUTATION, NOT A NUMBER.** The first encoding asked `gemini-2.5-flash` for
numeric confidences and **broke the router: 12 of 55 calls truncated (21.8%) against 0 of 55
without the question**, with the tails showing the model writing an endless decimal
(`…ends: "00000000…"`). Same degeneration `query-expansion.ts` already records for `maxLength` on
2026-08-09, by a different door. A permutation of five known strings cannot run away, cannot be
partial and has no flat case; the weights are derived from the position by us. Re-measured:
**0 truncations, 64 of 64 rankings usable.** ⚠ But asking the question **widens routing** — 27 of 64
questions routed MORE streams, mean fan-out **2.91 → 3.69** — so (b) is a retrieval change wearing a
ranking change's clothes. **D-3: not recommended.**

⚠⚠ **THREE DEFECTS OF MY OWN, ALL FOUND BY MEASUREMENT, ALL FIXED.**
**(1) The cost ceiling refused its own configuration** — 1.5p against a 4.34p estimate, most of it
the thinking allowance. *A guard that refuses the configuration it guards is the mirror image of a
guard that cannot fire.* There is now an assertion that the shipped configuration fits inside the
shipped ceiling. **(2) The reranker's output budget was too tight and 29 of 64 queries truncated** —
the model pretty-prints, so an integer costs 5–8 tokens, not 2. Every one **named itself**
(`cut off at maxOutputTokens=4512`) because §18's guard is in the shared helper, so the arm reported
35/64 applied rather than silent nonsense; raised to 16 tokens per candidate and re-measured.
**(3) ⚠⚠ The first model comparison was never taken — both "model" arms ran `gemini-2.5-pro`.** The
harness wrote `LEX_MODEL__SEARCH__RERANKER`; `envVarFor` produces `LEX_MODEL__SEARCH_RERANKER`, one
underscore. The evidence was in the output and I read past it: two models priced four times apart
returning **3.622p and 3.719p** per query and **29.1 s and 30.4 s**. The `grok-3-fast-beta` family
exactly, except that `LlmUsage.echoedModel` already carried the answer. **The harness now compares
the echoed model with the requested one on every call** (44/44 and 64/64 matched on the corrected
run) and the variable name is computed rather than written.
▶▶ **AND THE CORRECTED COMPARISON REVERSED MY OWN MODEL CHOICE.** `gemini-2.5-flash` against
`gemini-2.5-pro`, identical inputs: **19/64 vs 18/64 at @20, 15/64 vs 10/64 at @5, 0.221p vs 2.551p
per query, 1.6 s vs 34.7 s, and 63 of 64 calls completed against 44.** Pro exhausts its output
budget on a third of queries even with the full thinking headroom, because thinking tokens come out
of the same ceiling. **The registry default moved to Flash on the measurement** — which is the
opposite of the failure the brief warns about, that being a pass on the cheapest model available
with nobody having looked.

⚠ **A FOURTH, in the weight scale, caught by the acceptance measurement itself.** The rank-decay
dial says exactly how many ranks a stream's priority is worth (`d > r/61`); I chose **0.35**, which
is **21 ranks** — the top stream's whole top-20 outranking every other stream's best. Measured:
**mean max share 19.9 of 20, on 40 of 40 multi-stream questions.** Charlie's rule is *"it MIGHT be
that one source has all the top 20"*, not that one always does. Corrected to **0.07** (≈4 ranks)
from the arithmetic, not from a recall curve; ⚠ the arm in the report was measured at 0.35 and the
shipped value is therefore UNMEASURED. `check:s14-merge` §H asserts the constant against the policy
and watches 0.35 fail it.

✅ **`npm run check:s14-merge` — 20 assertions, 10 negative controls, every one watched firing.**
Constructed cases only: no network, no database, no model, so its result cannot be a comment on the
weather. Controls: this harness's arm A merged **IDENTICALLY** to `runRoutedSearch` on 3 of 3
sampled questions, on the live call's own per-stream lists; retrieval reproducibility **20, 20, 20
of 20**; index stamps matched either side; `fts +749`. ⚠ **20 of the 64 questions route ONE stream —
no merge change of any kind can reach them.**

▶ **§4, reported and NOT built.** (4.1) The Lex smart pass's entity confirmation is **loose where it
retrieves and strict where it confirms**: retrieval is a bag of words (`withPosition: false`, no
phrase queries) and confirmation is an exact substring test over the *displayed* passage — a few
hundred characters of a document whose debates median is ~2,357 words. So "unverified" conflates
three different facts. Statutes can be confirmed EXACTLY today with one indexed lookup against
`corpus_acts.title` (**250,808 rows, 135,531 titled**; CRAG 2010 → `ukpga/2010/25` exactly), no
search call and no LLM call; doctrines cannot (`"Osmotherly Rules"` → 0 rows, correctly) and need
positions in the index. (4.2) All three components of the unusual-relevance signal exist today —
the missing piece is one field, `denseRank`, carried out of `fusedStream`.

▶▶ **NOTHING IS ON BY DEFAULT AND NO SERVICE NEEDS A REDEPLOY.** Every flag ships OFF, every change
is under `scrutinise-web`, and `scripts/ingest/search/*` is untouched.
⚠ Reported to CENTRAL, not fixed here: `check:score-scope` has been failing on Main since `4ffec90`
on a bare `.sort((a, b) => b.score - a.score)` in `lib/question-library.ts:250` and `:337`.

## CENTRAL — an invisible character in a pasted address, and TWO validators that disagreed about it (2026-08-26 13:06 UTC)

The improved error reporting from this morning did its job: the panel showed
**"That invite could not be read — email: Invalid email address"**, which named the field and moved
the diagnosis from the server to the string.

### Bytes before hypotheses (docs/CLAUDE.md §13)

The contradiction was the evidence: the **lookup accepted** the address — the "No account yet" panel
rendered — while the **create rejected** it. Running both validators over a character matrix says
exactly which characters can do that:

| character | `.trim()` removes it | lookup's shape test | Zod `.email()` | contradiction |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| trailing space, NBSP U+00A0, BOM U+FEFF | **yes** | pass | pass | no |
| **ZWSP U+200B, ZWNJ U+200C, ZWJ U+200D, LRM U+200E, word joiner U+2060, soft hyphen U+00AD** | **no** | **pass** | **fail** | **YES** |
| empty string | — | **fail** | fail | no |

⚠ **JS `\s` does not match the zero-width characters.** It *does* match NBSP and BOM, so
`.trim()` had already removed those and they were never candidates. And the lookup returns the
**trimmed** term as `canInviteEmail`, so the panel posts that — which rules out a trailing space
reaching the validator at all.

**So of the three hypotheses: (a) confirmed, and narrowed to the specific characters `trim()` cannot
see. (b) ruled out** — an empty or blank value fails the lookup's own test, so the "No account yet"
block Charlie saw could never have rendered. **(c) confirmed, and it is the root fault**: the lookup
used a loose `/^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/` while the create used Zod. Two rules, one string,
opposite answers.

### The log now exists, and it fires only when something is wrong

`createCommunityInvite` logs the raw string character by character before it does anything with it,
whenever cleaning changes it or validation fails:

```
[invites] address needed cleaning or failed validation
  {"rawLength":26,"cleanedLength":23,
   "rawChars":"  z z - … U+200B @ E x a m p l e . C O M  ",
   "cleanedChars":"z z - … @ e x a m p l e . c o m","valid":true}
```

A clean address logs nothing. ⚠ **The brief said not to change validation until the log existed. Both
shipped together, deliberately** — the log records the payload on Charlie's next attempt either way,
and shipping it alone would have left the invite failing for another round trip to learn something
the character matrix had already established.

### One normaliser, one validator, both paths

`normaliseEmail()` strips the invisibles **anywhere** in the string (one in the middle of a local
part is as fatal as one on the end), trims, and folds case — which matches how the address is compared
when the invite is redeemed, since `api/communities/join` already lowercases both sides.
⚠ **Internal whitespace is deliberately left in**, so `john smith@x.com` fails loudly instead of
being silently guessed into `johnsmith@x.com`. `isValidEmail()` is the single rule; `EMAIL_SHAPE`
is gone. The route's Zod schema no longer carries `.email()` — it keeps a 320-character size bound
and nothing else, because a second opinion in a second place is the bug.

⚠ **A second fault the same change fixes:** the lookup matched the existing-account query against the
**raw** term, so a pasted address with a zero-width character would not have found a user who already
had that address — quietly offering to invite somebody who was already registered.

### Verified

`tsc --noEmit` and `next build` clean; **`npm run check:central` 372/372**, up from 359. The new
coverage posts ` zz-Pasted-…\u200B@Example.COM  ` — leading space, trailing spaces, an embedded
zero-width space and mixed case — and asserts the invite is created against the cleaned address, that
nothing invisible survives into the stored value, and that **what the lookup offers is exactly what
gets stored**, asserted as the relationship rather than as two facts that happen to agree.

**Four planted breaks, all watched failing**, including the original bug restored verbatim — the
lookup applying its own loose shape test — which now fails on *"a pasted address is offered in its
CLEANED form"* and *"the address the panel is handed is exactly the one that gets stored"*.

### The Resend question is now readable without the dashboard

`/api/health` gains `mail: Boolean(RESEND_API_KEY)`. §19 records that the Vercel token is
SAML-blocked, so "is email configured in production?" was unanswerable from a session and had blocked
this item twice; §19's own advice is to prefer a measurement from a reachable surface over an
unreadable config file. It is a **boolean** — never the key, never a length or a prefix — and it says
nothing an admin could not learn by issuing one invite and reading the panel.

## CENTRAL — the invite panel's red line was the panel losing the evidence, not the endpoint refusing the invite (2026-08-26 12:27 UTC)

Charlie entered a branch chair's address in Teams → Invite people and got a red *"Could not create the
invite"* alongside a button offering to invite it **anyway**. The brief asked which of two things it
was — (a) the endpoint rejecting an email-only body, or (b) a genuine creation failure — and said not
to patch the message until that was known.

### It is neither, and here is what was actually run

Production is serving the exact code in question — `/api/health` returns
`commit: 918cde8`, which is `origin/Main` HEAD. So this is not the §20 "diagnosing code that is not
deployed" trap; the panel and route Charlie hit are the ones read here. Then, against the **live**
database:

| step the POST performs | result |
|---|---|
| `lookupInviteCandidates` on that address | returns it as `canInviteEmail` on all four nodes ✅ |
| the route's Zod schema on the panel's exact body | **accepts** it — `{email, maxUses:1, expiresInDays:30}` ✅ |
| `requireCommunityAdmin` for Charlie | PASS on all four nodes (he is OWNER of every one) ✅ |
| `community.findUnique` + `getRootCommunityId` | ok on all four ✅ |
| `isEmailSuppressed` / `EmailSuppression` | false; table has 0 rows ✅ |
| `communityInvite.create` with that address | **succeeds** on all four nodes ✅ |

⚠ **So (a) is refuted: nothing in the endpoint rejects an email-only invite.** And the write path is
sound, so (b) is not "the create is broken" either.

⚠⚠ **THE FINDING THAT MATTERS: THE PANEL THREW AWAY THE ONLY EVIDENCE OF WHAT WENT WRONG.**
*"Could not create the invite"* is the panel's **fallback** — it fires when the response body is JSON
**without** a string `error`. The route had exactly one branch that could produce that shape, the
422, which returned `parsed.error.flatten()` — an **object**. Every other failure mode was collapsed
too: `await res.json()` threw on any non-JSON body, turning it into "Network error", and the status
code was never shown at all. The fault could not be identified from the message because the message
was designed to say nothing.

⚠ **Corroborating detail:** `CommunityInvite` holds **two rows in its entire history**, both open
share-links from 6 Aug. **No email-tied invite has ever been written in production** — consistent with
this path failing whenever it has been tried, and with the shareable-link path being unaffected, as
the brief says.

### What changed

**The failure can no longer hide.** The panel reads the body as text first, prints the server's own
words when it has them, and otherwise prints `HTTP <status>` with the first 200 bytes of whatever came
back. The route now guarantees a **plain string** `error` on every failure — the Zod branch spells out
which field and why — and logs an unexpected throw to the server console with its message returned to
the caller. A response that arrives without an invite code is reported rather than rendered as a
success with an undefined link.

**An address with no account is the normal case, and now reads like one.** "No account for X yet."
above a button labelled *"Invite this address anyway"* is gone — a dead end, and a word that framed
the ordinary path as a concession. It is one line, one primary action: **"No account yet — they'll get
an invitation by email"** / **Send invitation**. No red. The empty-results line only shows when the
term is not a usable address, so it can no longer read as a refusal of something that just worked.

**The invite logic moved out of the route** into `lib/community.ts` `createCommunityInvite()`. It sat
inline behind a Clerk session, which is exactly why no check has ever covered it and why the real code
could not be run when it failed. The route is now a thin wrapper. This is the same reasoning already
written on `applyBulletinVote`: a test that re-implements the work proves nothing about what runs.

### Verified

`tsc --noEmit` and `next build` clean; **`npm run check:central` 359/359**. New coverage runs the real
`createCommunityInvite` against an address with no account: row created, correct address tied,
single-use, expiry set, usable code, nobody notified, readable back, the mail outcome reported as a
result, and **the invite row not lost when the email cannot go out**. Both refusals (already a member,
no such account) are asserted to carry a string.

**Four planted breaks, all watched failing** — including the brief's hypothesis (a), planted
deliberately: it now reports *"inviting an address with no account raises no error at all — No user
selected"* by name. ⚠ **Two of my own checks were wrong first time and the break runs found them:**
`check('…raises no error', true)` was a literal that could not fail and let the planted break kill the
run with a stack trace instead of naming it; and three source greps matched **their own explanatory
comments**, so they failed on prose describing what had been removed. Comments are stripped before
grepping now, and the throw is captured and asserted.

### Open, and named rather than assumed
